Collection: Evacuation Chairs and Rescue Stretchers

Primary: evacuation chair (600/mo). Secondary: evac chair (500), evacuation chairs for stairs (150), emergency evacuation chair (100), stair evacuation chair (90), emergency stair chair (90), evacuation wheelchair (80), evacuation sled (80), rescue chair (50). Ricky's note: keep stair evacuation chair and emergency evacuation chair on this page; the collection also covers rescue stretcher (200).
Work Place Safety - Evacuation Chairs & Stretchers
Headings marked [H2] should be set as H2 on the page.
[H2] Evacuation Chairs for Stairs, Evacuation Sleds, and Rescue Stretchers

moves a person who cannot walk down the stairs safely when the elevators are out of service, during a fire, power outage, earthquake, or medical emergency. Anchortex carries Evac+Chair stair evacuation chairs, powered stair climbing chairs, evacuation sleds, and accessories, along with Rapid Extraction (REX) rescue stretchers, for hospitals, nursing homes, schools, offices, high-rise buildings, and correctional facilities.

Most evac chair models are operated by one person: the passenger sits in a secure seat while the operator guides the chair down the stairs on tracks or belts that control the speed. Some models also carry a passenger up the stairs. An evacuation chair can be used in place of an evacuation wheelchair on stairs, where a standard wheelchair cannot go.

Evac+Chair 300H, 400H, 600H, and 750H stair evacuation chairs for controlled travel down the stairs, with weight capacities from 400 to 500 lbs. The 600H and 750H also have extra handles so two people can carry a passenger up the stairs.
The battery powered Evac+Chair Power 800 and Power 900 carry a passenger up or down the stairs with one operator, for emergency evacuation and daily patient transport.
The IBEX 700H Tran-Seat lets two people move a patient up and down the stairs without carrying or heavy lifting.
The Evac+Sled, the Ulti-Mat (standard and bariatric sizes), and the Evac+Sheet rescue sheet, which stays under the mattress, for moving people who cannot sit, or bedridden patients, down the stairs.
REX ONE, REX DCS with descent control for stairs and steep ground, and REX DCS/CF for correctional facilities. Each folds in three for storage and lets one responder move a patient.
Comfy Seat cushions, the Transporter seat for transfers from a wheelchair, metal storage cabinets, anti-theft alarms, and the iEvac smoke and fire escape hood.
[H2] How to Choose an Evacuation Chair
Check the rated capacity against the people who may need it. The 750H is rated to 500 lbs, and the Ulti-Mat comes in a bariatric size
Most models need one trained operator; some need two, and some allow two-person carrying when needed
Manual evacuation chairs are made for going down the stairs. For going up, choose a powered stair chair, the IBEX 700H, or a model with carry handles
Measure the stair landings and plan where each chair will be kept. Wall mounting and storage cabinets keep chairs close to the stairs and ready to use
Train staff on the chair, practice regularly, and include it in the building's emergency action plan
A lightweight, folding stair chair that lets one or two operators move a person with limited mobility down the stairs, and with some models up the stairs, during an emergency.
How many people does it take to operate an evac chair?
Most manual Evac+Chair models and the powered Power 800 and Power 900 need one operator. The IBEX 700H needs two. Models with carry handles can be lifted by two people.
Can an evacuation chair go up the stairs?
Yes, with the right model. The powered Power 800 and Power 900 and the IBEX 700H go up and down the stairs. The 600H and 750H can be carried up by two people.
Where should evacuation chairs be kept?
Near the stairways, on a wall mount or in a storage cabinet, so staff can reach them quickly.

Evac+Chair has made stairway evacuation chairs since 1982, and its chairs were designed in the United States. Rapid Extraction designs and builds REX rescue stretchers in the U.S.A. Explore the full line of
Evacuation Chairs for Stairs and Rescue Stretchers at Anchortex
Work Place Safety - Evacuation Chairs & Stretchers at Anchortex
Shop evacuation chairs for stairs from Evac+Chair, plus evacuation sleds and REX rescue stretchers for safe emergency evacuation of mobility impaired people.

Anchortex's Evacuation Chairs & Stretchers are designed for safe patient transport during emergencies, including mobility‑assisted evacuation solutions for hospitals and other facilities. Shop Anchortex!

Keywords: this page uses Ricky's primary keyword "evacuation chair" in the H1 area, the first sentence, a heading and the FAQs, and the secondary keywords evac chair, evacuation chairs for stairs, emergency evacuation chair, stair evacuation chair, evacuation wheelchair, evacuation sled, and rescue stretcher. "Emergency stair chair" (90) and "rescue chair" (50) are not used yet; tell me if you want them worked in.

H1: the collection title is "Work Place Safety - Evacuation Chairs & Stretchers". I suggest "Evacuation Chairs and Rescue Stretchers". If "Work Place Safety -" is needed for your menus or other collections, we can keep it in the title and change only the SEO title.

Evacuation wheelchair: Andrew suggested "The REX chair can be used instead of an evacuation wheelchair in some circumstances." REX is a stretcher, so I wrote it about evacuation chairs ("An evacuation chair can be used in place of an evacuation wheelchair on stairs, where a standard wheelchair cannot go"). Please check this is what you meant.

Capacities: I used only what our product pages say: 300H 400 lbs, 400H 440 lbs, 750H 500 lbs. The Power 900 page says 560 lbs, but the Evac+Chair website says "up to 500lbs", so I left powered chair capacities out of this page.

Power 400H: our product name says "Power 400H", but the Evac+Chair website lists the 400H as a manual chair (440 lbs), and our page describes it for downward evacuation. I listed it with the manual chairs. Is the 400H powered?
Names: the Evac+Chair website does not use "Power 1-800" (it says Power 800), "Transporter", "Evac+Alarm", or "Rescue Sheet" (it says Evac+Sheet). I used the website names on this page.
REX DCS/CF: the Rapid Extraction website lists only REX ONE and REX DCS. The CF (correctional facility) version is described on our product page only.
FAQs: I added four short FAQs, because buyers search these questions and the Evac+Chair website answers them. Tell me if you want them on the collection page or left out.
Links: there is an Evac+Chair collection, but no Rapid Extraction collection, so I linked only to Evac+Chair.
Process: How I Optimize a Page with Keywords

take the primary keyword, secondary keywords and Ricky's note for the page. The primary goes in the H1 or first sentence, the SEO title, the meta description, one heading, and the FAQs. Secondary keywords go where they read naturally. Keywords Ricky reserved for another page are not reused.
add Andrew's points and notes. For example, we don't sell an evacuation wheelchair, so that term is used only to explain what an evacuation chair does instead.

search the primary keywords and review the pages that rank (retailers, the manufacturer, buyer guides): what they cover, whether they have FAQs and which questions, and which keywords they use in product names.
every spec comes from our own product pages and the manufacturer's website or spec sheet. Where they disagree, I leave the number out and list the conflict in the notes for Andrew.

a clear H1, a short intro, scannable bullets, H2 sections (types, how to choose, FAQs, about the brand), links to our collection pages only, an SEO title of 50 to 65 characters and a meta description of 140 to 160 characters. Copy reads like a person wrote it, with no claims comparing us to other brands.
the draft goes into this doc with notes and questions. Andrew comments, and Ricky reviews how the keywords and selling points were used.
I update Shopify one page at a time, keeping the URL, SKUs and prices, then check the live page against the approved draft (text, SEO fields, headings, links, weights).
Collection Page Pilot: What the Research Found
Who ranks for "evacuation chair" and "evacuation chairs for stairs":
manufacturers (Stryker, Evac+Chair), retailers (Grainger, Rehabmart, Global Industrial, Staples), and university and city buyer guides (NYC Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities, UC Berkeley).
they put the capacity in the product name (for example "Evacuation Chair, 500 lb. Capacity"). Their category copy is thin, and the pages we could read had no FAQs.
Buyer guides and the manufacturer FAQ:
they answer the same questions: how many operators, can it go up the stairs, capacity, stairway type, storage, training, and emergency action plans.
a "Types" section, a "How to choose" section, and four FAQs based on those questions, answered with facts from our product pages and the Evac+Chair website.
consider adding the capacity to product names or subtitles, as the retailers do (Andrew to decide).
